title: Ozempic and Wegovy May Carry a Hair-Loss Risk for Some Men
excerpt: A new NYU Langone study finds the first genetic link between GLP-1 drugs and male-pattern hair loss — but researchers stress the evidence is early and applies only to men already genetically predisposed.
body:
• Men already genetically predisposed to pattern baldness face roughly 7% higher odds of hair loss if they use GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic, Wegovy, or Zepbound, according to a new NYU Langone Health study.
  • The study, published September 3 in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology, is the first to show a genetic link between GLP-1 receptor activity and male-pattern hair loss — but it did not study actual drug users.
  • Researchers stress the evidence is early: they analyzed a biological pathway via genetics, not the medications themselves, and the findings apply only to men.
  • Rapid weight loss remains the leading explanation for shedding reported by GLP-1 users, and hair often regrows once weight stabilizes.

The most effective weight-loss drugs ever developed may come with a catch for some men. Ozempic, Wegovy, and Zepbound could carry an additional risk of hair loss for men already genetically predisposed to baldness, according to a study published September 3 in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology.

Led by researchers at NYU Langone Health, the study found that genetic variants associated with naturally higher levels of GLP-1 receptor proteins — the same receptors these drugs activate — are more common in men with androgenetic alopecia, the inherited pattern hair loss that affects the top and front of the scalp. Each standard step up in a man's genetically predicted receptor level was associated with roughly 7% higher odds of pattern baldness. The association held even after the researchers adjusted for other known hair-loss contributors, including hypertension, BMI, blood pressure, and lower testosterone.

"Our study provides the first genetic link between GLP-1 use and an increased risk of male-pattern hair loss from androgenetic alopecia, an association long suspected but until now not shown scientifically."

— Lynn Petukhova, senior investigator and geneticist, NYU Grossman School of Medicine

How the study worked — and its limits

The team used a technique called two-sample Mendelian randomization, which uses naturally occurring genetic differences as stand-ins for biological exposure. They identified 22 genetic variants that increase expression of GLP1R, the gene encoding the GLP-1 receptor, and compared them against genetic data on androgenetic alopecia. Crucially, the researchers did not follow anyone taking GLP-1 medications.

"The most important distinction is that we studied a biological pathway, not the medications themselves."

— Ravi Ramessur, post-doctoral research fellow, University of Pennsylvania, and study co-author

That caveat is the study's central limit. Genetically increased GLP1R expression is not the same as taking a GLP-1 drug at a particular dose for a particular period, Ramessur told Inc. The study also looked only at men, because the genetics of male-pattern hair loss are far better understood than the female form. "Large genetic studies of female pattern hair loss do not yet exist. So we cannot yet say whether the same relationship exists in women," Petukhova said.

Weight loss remains the main suspect

Hair thinning has been reported by both men and women taking GLP-1 drugs. Until now, researchers have largely attributed that shedding to the rapid weight loss the medications drive — a phenomenon known as telogen effluvium — and many users report hair regrowing several months after their weight stabilizes. The new findings do not overturn that explanation; they add a possible genetic layer beneath it.

A separate large multicenter cohort study from George Washington University researchers, published in JAAD International and based on data from nearly 550,000 patients, also found GLP-1 users had a higher risk of non-scarring hair loss at 12 months compared with matched controls — independent of age, sex, BMI, and diabetes status — suggesting the risk may not be explained by dieting alone.

What to watch

Researchers see a path toward doctors one day screening patients genetically before prescribing GLP-1 drugs, but that day is not here. For now, dermatologists say anyone noticing unusual shedding should tell their doctor rather than stopping treatment on their own — the cardiovascular and metabolic benefits of these medications far outweigh a cosmetic side effect for most patients. More direct studies, following actual drug users over time, will be needed before the 7% figure becomes clinical guidance.
